paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown was born in 1716 at Kirkharle, Northumberland, in north-east England. He went to the village school and then began work as a gardener on the Kirkharle Estate, then owned by the Loraine family, who seem to have been very supportive of Brown and encouraged his talent. Brown left Kirkharle at the age of 23, and within two years was head gardener to Lord Cobham at Stowe in Buckinghamshire. It was during his time at Stowe that Brown began working as an independent garden designer and contractor.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Brown grew up at a time when British garden designers looked to Europe for inspiration. They admired neat and symmetrical layouts, modelling their creations on French gardens, such as those at the palace of Versailles near Paris. But by the time Brown was made head gardener at Stowe, this had started to change, and taste for a more natural landscape developed. The so-called 'English style' can be seen as a reaction against the formality found in the designs of European gardens. But there was another factor involved. Rich men with access to the new technologies of surveying and drainage could now improve their own 'natural' landscape.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Brown’s designs connected the grand house, parkland and countryside in an unbroken flow. He did not seek to alter the appearance of the natural landscape very radically; rather he aimed to enhance and perfect what was already there. This is evident in the way he favoured native trees such as oak, elm, ash and beech. Tree planting was a significant ingredient of Brown’s improvements. Because trees take so long to mature, Brown invented a tree-moving machine to transplant mature specimens, so that his clients could get immediate results. Planting trees in gardens or parks seems to us now so obviously a force for good that it is hard for us to understand what a novel practice it was before the 18th century. Some of his contemporaries were very critical of Brown’s seemingly natural landscapes. The architect William Chambers wrote that Brown’s landscapes differed ‘very little from common fields, so closely is nature copied in most of them’.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: But in fact there was a great deal of disguised artifice involved in Brown’s works and he was not afraid to take extreme steps in order to achieve his vision. Frequently, the fine-tuning of a natural landscape required a great deal of human intervention. A project would typically take around five years to complete and would involve teams of labourers to dig, drain and move the soil into place. He installed what were known as ‘ha-has’, sunken ditches which prevented the best vistas from being obscured by hedges or fences. He ordered enormous mature trees to be transplanted, buildings to be removed and valleys to be flooded. He even recommended that whole villages be moved to different locations.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: ‘Capability’ Brown offered a number of different services to his clients: he could simply provide a survey and plans for buildings and landscape, and leave his client to execute his proposal; but more frequently he also sent a foreman to oversee the project, which would be carried out by labour recruited from the estate. In 1753, Brown was employing four foremen, and by the end of the decade he had over twenty foremen on his books. Alternatively, for a higher fee, Brown could oversee and refine the work himself, usually by visiting the estate for a certain number of days each year.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: It has been estimated that Brown created some 267 designs over his enthusiastically 40-year career. His skill in identifying and then exploiting a landscape's capability has given him the nickname 'Capability' Brown, by which he is still known today. Brown's reputation depended on his immense knowledge of plants and planting as well as his ability to make use of innovative methods for drainage and building dams. However, unique as it was Brown's vision for how a landscape should look that made him the designer of choice for Britain's wealthiest landowners, culminating in his appointment as Master Gardener to the king.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The image of the ideal English landscape, created by Brown, is as deeply rooted in the English character as are the works of the greatest English artists and poets. 'Capability' Brown is still celebrated today for the immense scale of his landscapes; his ambitious garden designs almost always involved large stretches of woodland and the creation of a lake. Although his work is not always admired today, most major landscape gardeners and landscape architects since, both in Britain and across the world, have been influenced in one way or another by Brown. Over two centuries have passed since his death, but such are the enduring qualities of his work that over 150 of the landscapes with which he is associated remain worth seeing today.
